faq.q: Can any snake be identified from a photo?
faq.a: Photo identification works best with a clear, well-lit picture of the whole snake taken from a safe distance (at least two metres). Blurry, dark or partial photos reduce accuracy, and some species look very alike. Treat every result as a guide, not a guarantee.
It can be wrong. The result comes from an AI model, not a herpetologist, and no accuracy figure is claimed. If a snake has bitten someone, treat it as an emergency whatever the result says.

faq.q: What should I do if someone has been bitten?
faq.a: Call 108 (ambulance) or 112 straight away, keep the person calm and the bitten limb still, remove rings and tight items, and go to a hospital. Do not cut the bite, suck out venom, tie a tight tourniquet or use herbal remedies.

faq.q: Should I catch or kill the snake so doctors can see it?
faq.a: No. Trying to catch or kill the snake leads to more bites. If it is safe, take a photo from a distance. Doctors treat according to the symptoms, so a photo helps but is not required.

faq.q: Does the app show where antivenom is in stock?
faq.a: No app can guarantee live stock. After a venomous result, VenomSnake lists the nearest hospitals from OpenStreetMap data, with phone numbers where available. Call ahead to confirm, or call 108, as ambulance crews often know which nearby hospital treats snakebite.

Photos are sent to Google's Gemini AI to be analysed and are not stored by VenomSnake. Google's own policies apply to data sent to its API. Results are saved only in your own browser so you can revisit them.
The interface is available in English and Hindi, with partial support for several other Indian languages. AI results are written in the language you select.
